questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 2 weeks. The ulcer has indurated edges and a clean base. Dark-field microscopy shows motile spirochetes. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (Hunterian chancre) is treated with Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. This is the first-line treatment per WHO/CDC guidelines. Doxycycline is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops a butterfly-shaped erythema over both cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive (1:640) with anti-dsDNA antibodies. Which complement pathway finding is most characteristic of this condition?
questions.exp: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) activates the classical complement pathway via immune complex deposition, leading to consumption of both C3 and C4. Both are typically low during active disease, distinguishing it from conditions that activate only the alternative pathway (low C3, normal C4).

questions.q: A 55-year-old farmer from rural Maharashtra presents with a chronic painless swelling of the foot with multiple sinuses discharging yellow granules. There is no lymphadenopathy. X-ray shows extensive bone destruction. Which organism is the most likely causative agent?
questions.exp: Madura foot (eumycetoma) with black/yellow granules in India is most commonly caused by Madurella mycetomatis, a true fungus. Yellow granules are seen in eumycetoma caused by Madurella mycetomatis. Actinomadura madurae (actinomycetoma) produces white to pale yellow granules.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the right side of the trunk following a dermatomal distribution. He complains of burning pain that preceded the rash by 3 days. The most appropriate antiviral therapy to reduce the risk of postherpetic neuralgia is:
opts: Acyclovir 200 mg 5 times daily for 5 days
Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Valacyclovir 1000 mg TID for 7 days achieves higher bioavailability than acyclovir and is superior in reducing duration of postherpetic neuralgia. It should be started within 72 hours of rash onset. Famciclovir 500 mg TID is also equivalent but valacyclovir is preferred for better compliance.

questions.q: A patient presents with hypopigmented macules on the trunk with loss of sensation. Slit skin smear shows acid-fast bacilli with a bacterial index of 3+. According to WHO classification, this patient should receive:
questions.exp: A BI of 3+ indicates multibacillary (MB) leprosy. WHO MB-MDT consists of rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine for 12 months. PB MDT (rifampicin + dapsone for 6 months) is for paucibacillary disease (BI 0). The 24-month regimen was used previously but was replaced by the current 12-month WHO regimen.

questions.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with tense blisters over the trunk and flexures with intense pruritus. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone. The target antigen is located in the:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid involves autoantibodies against BP180 (BPAG2/collagen XVII) located in the lower lamina lucida and BP230 (BPAG1) located in the hemidesmosome. However, BP180 is the primary pathogenic antigen in the lower lamina lucida. Type VII collagen (anchoring fibrils) is the antigen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 45-year-old presents with a pearly nodule on the nose with rolled borders, telangiectasias, and central ulceration. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels and spoke-wheel structures. The most common histological subtype of this tumour is:
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common subtype (~60-70% of cases), presenting as a pearly nodule with rolled borders and telangiectasias on sun-exposed areas. Morpheaform is the most aggressive subtype. Dermoscopy showing arborizing vessels and spoke-wheel areas is characteristic of BCC.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man presents with multiple soft, pedunculated perianal warts. PCR confirms HPV type 6. The patient is on antiretroviral therapy with CD4 count of 350 cells/μL. The best treatment to prevent recurrence is:
questions.exp: Imiquimod 5% cream (immune response modifier) is preferred in immunocompromised patients as it boosts local cell-mediated immunity, leading to lower recurrence rates compared to ablative therapies. It is applied 3 times weekly for up to 16 weeks. Podophyllotoxin is avoided in immunosuppressed patients for extensive lesions.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, puffy fingers, and dysphagia. Nailfold capillaroscopy shows giant capillary loops with haemorrhages and avascular areas. ANA is positive for anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I). This pattern indicates:
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) with higher risk of interstitial lung disease and renal crisis. Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome). The scleroderma pattern on capillaroscopy confirms SSc.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with annular scaly plaques on the trunk. KOH preparation shows septate hyphae and no arthrospores. Dermatophyte test medium shows a red colour change. The most appropriate topical antifungal for this condition is:
questions.exp: Terbinafine (allylamine) is fungicidal against dermatophytes and has the highest cure rates for tinea corporis due to its activity against dermatophyte cell wall ergosterol synthesis (squalene epoxidase inhibition). Azoles (ketoconazole, clotrimazole) are fungistatic. Terbinafine requires shorter treatment duration.

questions.q: A neonate born at term develops a widespread vesiculopustular eruption on the second day of life. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. HSV PCR is positive. The recommended treatment is:
opts: Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 14 days
Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 21 days
Valacyclovir 1 g orally TID for 14 days
Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 14 days
questions.exp: Neonatal HSV disease (disseminated or CNS involvement) is treated with acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 21 days. Skin-eye-mouth (SEM) disease requires 14 days. Oral valacyclovir cannot achieve adequate CNS levels in neonates. Higher doses (20 mg/kg vs 10 mg/kg) are required in neonates due to differences in drug distribution.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a 2 cm pigmented lesion on his back. Dermoscopy reveals irregular pigment network, regression structures, and blue-white veil. The Breslow thickness on histology is 2.5 mm with no ulceration. According to AJCC 8th edition, the T stage is:
questions.exp: According to AJCC 8th edition melanoma staging: T3 = 2.01-4.0 mm Breslow thickness. 'a' = no ulceration, 'b' = with ulceration. Since Breslow is 2.5 mm without ulceration, this is T3a. The blue-white veil on dermoscopy and irregular network are high-risk dermoscopic features suggesting melanoma.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. The pathergy test is positive. HLA typing shows HLA-B51 positivity. The most appropriate first-line treatment for this systemic condition is:
questions.exp: Behçet's disease (BD) — characterized by oral ulcers, genital ulcers, uveitis, and pathergy — is associated with HLA-B51. Colchicine is first-line for mucocutaneous manifestations (oral and genital ulcers, erythema nodosum). Azathioprine is used for ocular involvement. Thalidomide is effective for recalcitrant oral/genital ulcers but has significant side effects.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student presents with photosensitivity since childhood, multiple lentigines, skin cancers, and neurological deficits. Fibroblast culture shows deficient nucleotide excision repair. Which gene is most commonly mutated?
questions.exp: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is caused by mutations in nucleotide excision repair (NER) genes. XPC is the most commonly mutated gene in XP (complementation group C), accounting for ~25% of cases. XPA mutations are associated with the most severe neurological involvement. XPD mutations cause both XP and Cockayne syndrome overlap.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman with Type IV skin presents with malar hyperpigmentation worsened by oral contraceptive pills. Wood's lamp examination shows accentuation of pigment. This indicates primarily:
questions.exp: Wood's lamp (365 nm UVA) accentuates epidermal melanosis (increased contrast), as melanin in the epidermis strongly absorbs long-wave UV. Dermal melanin does not accentuate under Wood's lamp. Mixed type shows partial accentuation. OCP-triggered melasma is common and Wood's lamp helps determine treatment depth.

questions.q: A 45-year-old presents with a 1.5 cm verrucous plaque on the lower leg of 15 years' duration. Biopsy shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, intraepidermal abscesses with neutrophils, and copper-coloured muriform cells (sclerotic bodies). The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous (melanin-containing) fungi, most commonly Fonsecaea pedrosoi in India. It presents with verrucous plaques on extremities, and sclerotic bodies (Medlar/copper penny bodies/muriform cells) are pathognomonic on histology. Sporothrix causes sporotrichosis with lymphocutaneous spread.

questions.q: A 60-year-old presents with fragile skin, blistering on minimal trauma, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation. Urine shows elevated uroporphyrins. The enzyme deficient in this condition is:
questions.exp: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is caused by deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD), the fifth enzyme in the heme biosynthetic pathway. It presents with photosensitive blistering, skin fragility, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation. Elevated urine uroporphyrins (type I) are diagnostic. Treatment includes phlebotomy and low-dose hydroxychloroquine.

questions.q: A 18-year-old presents for treatment of nodulocystic acne. She is started on isotretinoin. Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to isotretinoin therapy?
questions.exp: Previous isotretinoin therapy is not a contraindication; patients may require repeat courses for relapse. Absolute contraindications include pregnancy (teratogenic), uncontrolled hyperlipidaemia (TG >800 mg/dL risk of pancreatitis), and active hepatic disease. Prior therapy is permitted with appropriate washout period and monitoring.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with erythematous, indurated plaques over the proximal nail fold and periungual telangiectasias. Gottron's papules are present over the knuckles. Muscle enzyme CPK is elevated. The most specific antibody for this condition is:
questions.exp: Anti-Mi-2 antibodies are the most specific antibody for classic dermatomyositis (DM), associated with V-sign, shawl sign, Gottron's papules, and a good treatment response. Anti-Jo-1 is associated with antisynthetase syndrome (myositis + ILD + mechanic's hands). Anti-MDA5 is associated with amyopathic DM with severe ILD.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male homosexual presents with multiple grouped vesicles on the perianal area. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. He is HIV positive with CD4 count of 80 cells/μL. Appropriate management is:
opts: Acyclovir 400 mg TID suppression therapy lifelong
Foscarnet 40 mg/kg IV TID for 3 weeks
questions.exp: In HIV patients with CD4 <200 cells/μL and recurrent HSV-2, chronic suppressive therapy with acyclovir 400 mg TID (or valacyclovir 500 mg BD) is recommended to prevent frequent recurrences. Foscarnet is reserved for acyclovir-resistant HSV strains. Suppressive therapy also reduces HIV transmission risk.

questions.q: A 28-year-old patient with leprosy on MB-MDT develops sudden onset erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) with fever, neutrophilia, and new skin lesions. The drug of choice for acute severe ENL is:
questions.exp: Thalidomide is the gold standard treatment for ENL, especially in men and non-pregnant women, acting by inhibiting TNF-α production. It reduces skin lesions, fever, and neuritis within 1-2 days. Prednisolone is used when thalidomide is contraindicated (pregnant women, fertile women without contraception). Clofazimine has anti-inflammatory properties but slower onset.

questions.q: During a Mohs micrographic surgery for a 2 cm morpheaform BCC on the nose, the surgeon examines the horizontal frozen sections. The main advantage of Mohs surgery over wide local excision is:
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery allows examination of 100% of the surgical margin (peripheral and deep) using horizontal frozen sections, compared to conventional wide local excision that examines only 1-3% of margins using bread-loaf sectioning. This results in the lowest recurrence rates (1% for primary BCC) and maximum tissue conservation, critical for areas like the nose.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with a flare of widespread psoriasis after streptococcal pharyngitis. She has 0.5-2 cm salmon-pink papules and plaques over the trunk. The most appropriate initial treatment is:
opts: Topical clobetasol + penicillin V 500 mg BD for 10 days
questions.exp: Guttate psoriasis triggered by streptococcal infection responds excellently to narrowband UVB (NBUVB) phototherapy and is considered first-line for widespread guttate psoriasis. Streptococcal treatment (penicillin) may help prevent recurrences but does not treat the psoriasis flare. Methotrexate and cyclosporine are reserved for severe/unresponsive cases.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with a tender, fluctuant, inflammatory swelling of the upper lip with sinus formation and sulfur granule discharge. Gram stain shows gram-positive filamentous branching rods. Culture on blood agar at 37°C shows molar-tooth colonies. Treatment of choice is:
opts: Penicillin G 10-20 MU IV for 4-6 weeks followed by amoxicillin
questions.exp: Actinomycosis (caused by Actinomyces israelii, anaerobic gram-positive filamentous bacterium) presents with cervicofacial swelling, sinuses, and sulfur granules. Molar-tooth colonies on blood agar confirm Actinomyces. Treatment is high-dose IV penicillin G for 4-6 weeks followed by oral amoxicillin for 6-12 months. Co-trimoxazole is used for Nocardia (aerobic filamentous organism).

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which toxin is responsible for the superficial blistering in bullous impetigo?
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo is caused by Staphylococcus aureus phage group II producing exfoliative toxins A and B (ETA/ETB), which are serine proteases that cleave desmoglein-1 in the stratum granulosum, causing superficial blistering without inflammation. TSST-1 causes toxic shock syndrome. The same toxins (when disseminated) cause staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for discoid lupus presents for routine monitoring. Which investigation is MOST important in this patient's annual follow-up?
opts: Fundus examination and visual field testing
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible retinopathy (bull's eye maculopathy) due to accumulation in melanin-containing cells of the retinal pigment epithelium. Annual ophthalmological screening (fundus examination, visual fields, and OCT) is mandatory, especially after 5 years of use or cumulative dose >1000g. Screening prevents permanent visual loss.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with progressive dyspigmentation — white patches on the dorsum of hands, perioral area, and around the eyes — since 6 months. The patches are chalk-white with Wood's lamp accentuation. The patient is euthyroid. The most appropriate treatment for localized vitiligo is:
questions.exp: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.1%, pimecrolimus 1%) are first-line for localized vitiligo, especially on the face and flexures, as they are steroid-sparing and safe for long-term use. They inhibit T-cell activation reducing melanocyte destruction. NBUVB is preferred for generalized vitiligo. Surgical options (transplant) are for stable localized vitiligo refractory to medical treatment.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a scaly, well-demarcated plaque on the lower leg with a red border and central clearing. KOH shows hyphae. He also has tinea unguium. Terbinafine 250 mg daily is prescribed for 3 months. Which drug interaction is most important to consider?
questions.exp: Terbinafine is a potent CYP2D6 inhibitor and also affects CYP1A2 and CYP3A4. Co-administration with warfarin increases anticoagulant effect by reducing its metabolism, increasing bleeding risk. INR must be monitored. Rifampicin reduces terbinafine plasma levels (induces CYP enzymes) but is not clinically as significant. This interaction is most relevant in elderly patients on anticoagulation.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of non-pitting edema of the lips, tongue, and extremities since childhood. She has a family history of similar episodes. C1 esterase inhibitor level is markedly low. The drug used for acute attacks is:
questions.exp: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) due to C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency is bradykinin-mediated, NOT histamine-mediated, so antihistamines, adrenaline, and corticosteroids are INEFFECTIVE. Icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist) is the most specific treatment for acute HAE attacks, given as 30 mg SC. C1-INH concentrate or fresh frozen plasma are alternatives when icatibant is unavailable.

questions.q: A 28-year-old with HIV presents with a firm, non-tender, violaceous plaque on the hard palate and multiple similar lesions on the trunk. Biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces and RBC extravasation. The causative agent is:
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is caused by Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8/Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, KSHV). It presents with violaceous patches/plaques on skin and mucosa in immunocompromised patients. Histology shows spindle cell proliferation, slit-like vascular spaces, and RBC extravasation. AIDS-associated KS (epidemic KS) is the most aggressive form.
